title: Ludi. Certamen navium
titleEn: The Games Open and the Boat Race — Aeneid V.104–200
part: The Games Open and the Boat Race (V.104–200)
about: The ninth day after the offerings at Anchises' tomb has come, and the people of the neighbourhood crowd the shore, drawn by the news and by the name of Acestes, some to watch the Trojans and some ready to compete. The prizes are set out in the middle of the ring, tripods, garlands, palms, armour, purple robes and talents of silver and gold, and a trumpet opens the games. The first contest is a race between four ships picked from the fleet: Mnestheus in the Pristis, Gyas in the huge Chimaera, Sergestus in the Centaur and Cloanthus in the Scylla, and Virgil names the Roman families that would later claim these captains as ancestors. A rock far out to sea, marked with a green branch of holm-oak, is the turning-post. At the trumpet the ships leap away, and the shouting echoes back from the hills. Gyas leads, but as they near the rock his helmsman Menoetes, afraid of hidden reefs, keeps steering out to sea; Cloanthus slips past on the inside, and Gyas in his rage throws the old man overboard and takes the helm himself, while Menoetes clambers up onto the rock, spitting out sea water, and the Trojans laugh. Sergestus and Mnestheus now hope to pass Gyas, and Mnestheus, striding among his rowers, begs them, if they cannot win, at least to spare themselves the shame of coming in last. Virgil is rewriting the chariot race of Homer's games for Patroclus, in Iliad XXIII, as a contest of ships; the race ends in the next part.

sentences.t:
Exspectata dies aderat, nonamque serena
Auroram Phaethontis equi iam luce vehebant,
famaque finitimos et clari nomen Acestae
excierat;
sentences.l:
The awaited day was at hand, and the ninth
Dawn the horses of Phaethon now in clear light were bearing,
and rumour the neighbours and of famous Acestes the name
had called out;
sentences.i: The day they had waited for was at hand: the horses of Phaethon were already bringing up the ninth dawn in a cloudless light, and the news, and the name of famous Acestes, had brought the neighbouring people out;
sentences.n: A new paragraph: the ninth day that Aeneas fixed for the games earlier in the book has come. 'Exspectata' is a perfect passive participle, 'awaited'; 'dies' is feminine here, as it often is of an appointed day. 'aderat' is the imperfect of 'adsum', 'was at hand'. 'nonam… Auroram' is the object of 'vehebant', 'were carrying the ninth Dawn', and 'serena… luce' is an ablative, 'in clear light'. 'Phaethontis equi' are the horses of the Sun: Phaethon, 'the shining one', is used here as a name of the Sun himself; in the verse 'Phaethontis' has four syllables, Pha-e-thon-tis. 'fama' and 'nomen' are the two subjects of 'excierat', the pluperfect of 'excio', 'had called out'; 'finitimos' is a masculine plural adjective used as a noun, 'the neighbours'.

sentences.t:
laeto complerant litora coetu,
visuri Aeneadas, pars et certare parati.
sentences.l:
with a glad gathering they had filled the shores,
to see the Aeneadae, some also to compete ready.
sentences.i: they had filled the shore in a cheerful crowd, come to see the men of Aeneas, and some of them ready to compete as well.
sentences.n: 'complerant' is a shortened pluperfect for 'compleverant', 'they had filled'; its subject is the people roused in the clause before. 'laeto… coetu' is an ablative, 'with a glad throng'. 'visuri' is the future participle of 'video', expressing purpose: 'meaning to see'. 'Aeneadas' is the accusative plural of 'Aeneadae', 'the followers of Aeneas'. 'pars', 'a part, some', is in apposition to the understood subject and takes the plural 'parati' by sense; 'parati' governs the infinitive 'certare'. 'et' here means 'also'.

sentences.t:
Munera principio ante oculos circoque locantur
in medio, sacri tripodes viridesque coronae,
et palmae pretium victoribus, armaque et ostro
perfusae vestes, argenti aurique talenta;
sentences.l:
The prizes first before the eyes, and in the ring, are placed
in the middle, sacred tripods and green garlands,
and palms, the reward for the victors, and arms, and with purple
steeped garments, of silver and of gold talents;
sentences.i: First the prizes are set out where all can see them, in the middle of the ring: sacred tripods and green garlands, palm-branches as the victors' reward, armour, robes soaked in purple, and talents of silver and gold;
sentences.n: 'principio' is an adverbial ablative, 'first, to begin with'. 'locantur' is a present passive, 'are placed'; its subject 'munera' is then spelled out in the list that follows. 'circo… in medio' is 'in the middle of the ring', the open space where the contests are watched; 'circus' is any circular course or arena, not yet the Roman Circus. Tripods were standard prizes in Homer's games (Iliad XXIII). 'palmae' is nominative plural, with 'pretium' in apposition, 'the reward', and 'victoribus' a dative, 'for the victors'. 'armaque et… vestes' is 'both arms and robes'; 'ostro perfusae' means 'steeped in purple' ('ostrum', the purple dye). 'talenta' are talents, a Greek weight of precious metal, with the genitives 'argenti aurique'.

sentences.t: et tuba commissos medio canit aggere ludos.
sentences.l: and the trumpet, from the mound in the middle, sounds the games joined.
sentences.i: and from a mound in the middle the trumpet sounds the start of the games.
sentences.n: 'tuba' is the subject of 'canit', which here takes an accusative: 'sounds the games', i.e. announces them. 'commissos… ludos' is literally 'the games joined', i.e. begun: 'committere' is used of joining battle or opening a contest. 'medio… aggere' is an ablative of place, 'on (from) the mound in the middle' of the ring, a raised bank from which the signal is given.

sentences.t:
Prima pares ineunt gravibus certamina remis
quattuor ex omni delectae classe carinae.
sentences.l:
The first, well matched, enter with heavy oars the contests,
four, chosen from the whole fleet, keels.
sentences.i: Four evenly matched ships, picked from the whole fleet, open the contests, racing with heavy oars.
sentences.n: A new paragraph: the boat race, Virgil's version of the chariot race that opens Homer's games for Patroclus in Iliad XXIII. The subject is 'quattuor… carinae' in the second line, 'four keels', i.e. ships: the keel stands for the whole ship. 'Prima… certamina' is the object of 'ineunt', 'enter the first contests'; the plural stands for a single race. 'pares' agrees with 'carinae', 'evenly matched'. 'gravibus… remis' is an ablative of means. 'delectae' is a perfect participle, 'chosen', with 'ex omni… classe', 'out of the whole fleet'.

sentences.t:
Velocem Mnestheus agit acri remige Pristim,
mox Italus Mnestheus, genus a quo nomine Memmi;
sentences.l:
The swift, Mnestheus drives with keen crew, Pristis,
soon Italian Mnestheus, from whose name the clan of Memmius;
sentences.i: Mnestheus, who would soon be an Italian and from whose name the house of Memmius comes, drives the swift Pristis with an eager crew;
sentences.n: 'Velocem… Pristim' frames the line: 'the swift Pristis', an accusative in -im (as 'puppim', 'turrim'), the name of the ship, meaning a sea-monster or whale. 'acri remige' is an ablative of means; 'remex', 'oarsman', is singular for the whole crew. 'mox Italus' means 'soon (to be) Italian': the poet looks ahead to the Roman families who claimed descent from these Trojans. 'genus a quo nomine Memmi' is 'from whose name (comes) the clan of Memmius', with 'est' understood; 'Memmi' is the genitive of 'Memmius', in -i for -ii. The link is probably a play on sound: 'Mnestheus' recalls Greek 'mnesthai', 'to remember', and 'Memmius' Latin 'memini', 'I remember'.

sentences.i: Gyas drives the huge Chimaera, a vast hulk the size of a town, pushed on by young Trojans rowing in three banks, the oars rising in three tiers;
sentences.n: 'agit' is understood from line 116. 'ingentem… Chimaeram' is the object, the ship named after the fire-breathing monster; 'ingenti mole' is an ablative of description, 'of huge bulk', and the repetition 'ingentem… ingenti' stresses her size. 'urbis opus', 'a city's work', is in apposition: a ship as big as a town, or a task fit for a whole city. 'pubes… Dardana', 'the Trojan youth', is singular in form but takes the plural verb 'impellunt' by sense. 'triplici… versu' is 'in a triple row', i.e. three banks of oars, and 'terno… ordine', 'in threefold tier', says it again. The last clause has no connective (asyndeton).

sentences.t:
Sergestusque, domus tenet a quo Sergia nomen,
Centauro invehitur magna, Scyllaque Cloanthus
caerulea, genus unde tibi, Romane Cluenti.
sentences.l:
and Sergestus, from whom the house holds Sergian its name,
on the Centaur is borne, great, and on the Scylla Cloanthus,
dark-blue, whence the clan to you, Roman Cluentius.
sentences.i: Sergestus, from whom the Sergian house takes its name, rides in the great Centaur, and Cloanthus in the sea-blue Scylla, Cloanthus from whom your line descends, Cluentius of Rome.
sentences.n: 'domus tenet a quo Sergia nomen' is 'from whom the Sergian house holds its name': the Sergii were a Roman family (Catiline was one of them). 'Centauro… magna' is an ablative with 'invehitur', 'is carried on the great Centaur'; the ship is feminine (as 'navis' is), so the adjective is 'magna'. 'Scyllaque… caerulea' is likewise an ablative, with 'invehitur' understood for Cloanthus; 'caerulea' is 'dark blue', the colour of the sea. 'genus unde tibi' has 'est' understood, and 'tibi' is a dative of possession: 'from whom you have your descent'. 'Romane Cluenti' is a vocative: the poet turns to address a Roman of the Cluentian family (apostrophe).

sentences.i: Far out to sea, facing the foaming shore, there is a rock that is sometimes sunk and battered by swelling waves, when the winter north-westers blot out the stars;
sentences.n: A new paragraph, opening with 'Est', 'there is', the usual way of introducing a place in an epic description. 'spumantia contra / litora' is 'opposite the foaming shore', with the preposition 'contra' set between the adjective and its noun. 'quod' is a relative referring to 'saxum'; 'submersum' is a perfect participle, 'submerged', and 'tunditur' a present passive, 'is beaten', with 'tumidis… fluctibus' an ablative of means. 'olim' here means 'at times', not 'once'. 'ubi' stands late in its clause: 'when the wintry north-west winds hide the stars'. Greenough prints 'cori' with a small letter; it is the wind more often spelt 'Caurus' (The Latin Library has 'Cauri'), the north-west wind, plural here.

sentences.t:
tranquillo silet, immotaque attollitur unda
campus, et apricis statio gratissima mergis.
sentences.l:
in calm it is silent, and from the motionless is raised water
a plain, and for sun-loving a station most welcome, divers.
sentences.i: In calm weather it lies silent, a level space lifted above the still water, a favourite resting-place for sea-birds basking in the sun.
sentences.n: 'tranquillo' is a neuter adjective used as a noun, an ablative of time or circumstance: 'in calm weather'. 'immota… unda' is an ablative: the rock is raised out of, or above, the motionless water; 'attollitur' is a present passive, 'is lifted'. 'campus', 'a plain, a level surface', is in apposition to the rock, and so is 'statio', 'a station, resting-place', with 'est' understood. 'apricis… mergis' is a dative, 'for the sun-loving divers'; the 'mergus' is a diving sea-bird, a gull or cormorant, and 'apricus' means 'basking in the sun'. Elision: 'immotaque attollitur'.

sentences.t:
Hic viridem Aeneas frondenti ex ilice metam
constituit signum nautis pater, unde reverti
scirent, et longos ubi circumflectere cursus.
sentences.l:
Here a green, Aeneas, from a leafy holm-oak, turning-post
set up, a mark for the sailors, the father, whence to turn back
they might know, and where their long courses to bend round.
sentences.i: Here father Aeneas set up a green turning-post, a leafy holm-oak bough, as a mark for the sailors, so that they would know where to turn back and where to swing round on their long course.
sentences.n: 'metam' is the 'turning-post', a term from the chariot race, where the teams rounded a post and came back; 'viridem… metam' frames the line, and 'frondenti ex ilice' means 'from a leafy holm-oak' ('ilex', the evergreen oak). 'signum' is in apposition to 'metam', and 'nautis' is a dative. 'pater' is a title of honour for Aeneas as leader. 'scirent' is an imperfect subjunctive expressing purpose: 'so that they might know where to turn back from'; 'ubi circumflectere… cursus' depends on the same 'scirent', 'and where to bend round their long courses'. 'reverti' is the infinitive of the deponent 'revertor'.

sentences.t:
Tum loca sorte legunt, ipsique in puppibus auro
ductores longe effulgent ostroque decori;
sentences.l:
Then places by lot they choose, and themselves on the sterns, with gold
the captains far shine out, and with purple splendid;
sentences.i: Then they draw lots for their places, and the captains themselves stand on the sterns, shining from far off in their splendour of gold and purple;
sentences.n: 'loca sorte legunt' is 'they choose their positions by lot', their places in the starting line. 'ipsi… ductores' is the subject, 'the captains themselves', as against their crews; 'in puppibus', 'on the sterns', where a commander stood. 'auro… ostroque decori' is 'splendid with gold and purple': 'decori' is the nominative plural of the adjective 'decorus', and 'auro' and 'ostro' are ablatives. 'effulgent' is 'shine out'; 'longe' is 'far, from afar'.

sentences.t:
cetera populea velatur fronde iuventus,
nudatosque umeros oleo perfilsa nitescit.
sentences.l:
the rest with poplar is veiled leafage, the youth,
and, its bared shoulders with oil steeped, it gleams.
sentences.i: the rest of the young men are crowned with poplar leaves, and their bare shoulders glisten with oil.
sentences.n: The print has 'perfilsa', a misprint for 'perfusa', 'steeped, drenched' (The Latin Library prints 'perfusa'); the gloss follows 'perfusa'. 'cetera… iuventus', 'the rest of the youth', a collective singular, is the subject of both verbs; 'populea… fronde' is an ablative, 'with poplar leaves': the poplar was sacred to Hercules, the patron of athletes. 'velatur' is a passive with middle sense, 'is wreathed'. 'nudatos… umeros' is an accusative of respect with 'perfusa', 'drenched as to their bared shoulders'; 'oleo' is an ablative of means. Athletes were rubbed with oil. 'nitescit' is inceptive in form, 'begins to shine, gleams'.

sentences.t: Considunt transtris, intentaque brachia remis;
sentences.l: They sit down on the thwarts, and stretched are their arms to the oars;
sentences.i: They take their seats on the benches, arms stretched out to the oars;
sentences.n: 'transtris' is an ablative of place, 'on the rowing-benches'. 'intenta… brachia' has 'sunt' understood: 'their arms are stretched' to the oars, 'remis' being a dative. Greenough prints 'brachia' (the familiar spelling is 'bracchia'). 'intenta' is picked up by 'intenti' in the next line.

sentences.t:
intenti exspectant signum, exsultantiaque haurit
corda pavor pulsans, laudumque arrecta cupido.
sentences.l:
intent they await the signal, and the leaping drains
hearts a fear throbbing, and of praises roused desire.
sentences.i: taut and ready, they wait for the signal, their leaping hearts emptied by the hammering of fear and a quickened hunger for praise.
sentences.n: 'intenti' repeats 'intenta' from the line before: arms and men alike are strained. 'exsultantia… corda' is the object of 'haurit', 'drains, drinks up', a vivid verb for a feeling that empties the heart. The subjects are 'pavor pulsans', 'throbbing fear', and 'laudum… arrecta cupido', 'a roused desire for praise' ('laudum' is an objective genitive; 'arrecta', a perfect participle, 'pricked up, roused'); the verb is singular, agreeing with the nearer subject. Elision: 'intenti exspectant', 'exsultantiaque haurit'.

sentences.t:
Inde, ubi clara dedit sonitum tuba, finibus omnes,
haud mora, prosiluere suis;
sentences.l:
Then, when the clear gave its sound, the trumpet, from bounds all,
no delay, leapt forth their own;
sentences.i: Then, as soon as the trumpet rang out clear, they all shot forward from their marks without a moment's delay;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'ubi… dedit', with the perfect, means 'when, as soon as'. 'clara… tuba' is 'the clear-sounding trumpet', and 'dedit sonitum' 'gave its sound'. 'finibus… suis', split across the line, is an ablative of separation, 'from their starting-lines'. 'haud mora' is a parenthesis with 'fuit' understood, 'there was no delay'. 'prosiluere' is the -ere form of the perfect, 'prosiluerunt', 'they leapt forward'.

sentences.t:
ferit aethera clamor
nauticus, adductis spumant freta versa lacertis.
sentences.l:
strikes the sky the shout
of sailors; with arms drawn in, foam the straits overturned.
sentences.i: the sailors' shouting strikes the sky, and the churned water foams as their arms pull in on the oars.
sentences.n: 'aethera' is a Greek accusative singular, 'the upper air'. 'clamor… nauticus' is 'the sailors' shout', the adjective held over to the next line. 'adductis… lacertis' is an ablative absolute, 'the arms having been drawn in', i.e. at the pull of each stroke. 'freta versa', 'the overturned straits', is the water churned up by the oars; 'fretum', a strait, is used for the sea.

sentences.t:
Infindunt pariter sulcos, totumque dehiscit
convulsum remis rostrisque tridentibus aequor.
sentences.l:
They cleave together furrows, and the whole gapes open,
torn up by oars and by beaks three-toothed, sea.
sentences.i: Side by side they cut their furrows, and the whole surface of the sea gapes open, torn up by the oars and the three-pronged beaks.
sentences.n: 'Infindunt' is from 'infindo', 'to cleave into', a rare verb: the ships plough furrows in the water, a farming image. 'pariter' is 'together, side by side'. 'totum… aequor' frames the rest of the sentence, 'the whole level sea', subject of 'dehiscit', 'gapes, splits open'; 'convulsum' is a perfect participle, 'torn up'. 'remis rostrisque tridentibus' are ablatives of means; the 'rostrum' is the ram at a warship's prow, here 'three-toothed', with three prongs.

sentences.t:
Non tam praecipites biiugo certamine campum
corripuere, ruuntque effusi carcere currus,
nec sic immissis aurigae undantia lora
concussere iugis pronique in verbera pendent.
sentences.l:
Not so headlong, in a two-yoke contest, the plain
have snatched, and rush, poured out from the barrier, the chariots,
nor so, with the teams let loose, have charioteers the rippling reins
shaken, and bent forward over the lashes hang.
sentences.i: Not so headlong do chariots in a two-horse race seize on the plain and stream out of the starting-gate, nor do charioteers so shake out the rippling reins over teams let go, leaning forward to hang over the whip.
sentences.n: An extended simile, put negatively ('Non tam… nec sic', 'not so… nor so'): the ships go faster than racing chariots. The comparison is pointed, since Virgil has turned Homer's chariot race into a race of ships. 'biiugo certamine' is an ablative, 'in a contest of two-horse chariots' ('biiugus', 'two-yoked'; scanned bĭ-jŭ-gō). 'praecipites… currus' is the subject of both 'corripuere' and 'ruunt'; 'corripuere campum', 'have snatched up the plain', i.e. dashed over it, is a perfect in -ere used of what regularly happens. 'effusi carcere' is 'poured out from the starting-gate' ('carcer', the barrier of the circus). 'immissis… iugis' is an ablative absolute, 'the teams let go'; 'aurigae' is nominative plural, and 'undantia lora' 'the waving reins'. 'proni' is 'leaning forward', and 'in verbera' 'into their lashes'.

sentences.t:
Tum plausu fremituque virum studiisque faventum
consonat omne nemus, vocemque inclusa volutant
litora, pulsati colles clamore resultant.
sentences.l:
Then with the clapping and roar of men and the zeal of supporters
resounds all the grove, and the voice the shut-in roll
shores; struck, the hills with the shouting leap back.
sentences.i: Then the whole wood rings with the clapping and roaring of the men and the cheers of their partisans; the enclosed shore rolls the sound along, and the hills, struck by the shouting, throw it back.
sentences.n: 'virum' is the old genitive plural for 'virorum' (you have met it before), and 'faventum' is the genitive plural of the present participle 'favens', 'of those cheering (their side)'; 'studiis' means 'partisanship, eager support'. The three ablatives 'plausu fremituque… studiisque' give the cause of 'consonat', 'resounds'. 'inclusa… litora', 'the shut-in shores', i.e. the bay closed in by hills, is the subject of 'volutant', 'roll', a frequentative of 'volvo'. 'pulsati' is a perfect participle, 'struck'; 'resultant' is 'leap back, echo'. The last clause has no connective (asyndeton).

sentences.t:
Effugit ante alios primisque elabitur undis
turbam inter fremitumque Gyas;
sentences.l:
Escapes ahead of the others and over the foremost waves glides away,
the crowd amid and the roar, Gyas;
sentences.i: Gyas gets away ahead of the rest and slips out in front over the water, amid the crush and the uproar;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. The subject, 'Gyas', is held back to the end. 'primis… undis' is 'on the foremost waves', i.e. in the lead, an ablative of place or route. 'turbam inter fremitumque' is 'amid the crowd and the noise', with the preposition 'inter' placed after its first noun (anastrophe). 'elabitur' is from the deponent 'elabor', 'slip out, glide away'.

sentences.t:
quem deinde Cloanthus
consequitur, melior remis, sed pondere pinus
tarda tenet.
sentences.l:
whom next Cloanthus
follows, better in oars, but by weight the pine,
slow, holds back.
sentences.i: next comes Cloanthus, the better at the oars, but his ship is slow with her weight and holds him back.
sentences.n: 'quem' is a connecting relative, 'and him' (Gyas). 'consequitur' is deponent, 'follows close behind'. 'melior remis' is 'better in oars', an ablative of respect: his crew rows better. 'pinus', 'the pine', stands for the ship built of it; 'tarda… pondere' is 'slow because of its weight', and 'tenet' means 'holds him back'.

sentences.t:
Post hos aequo discrimine Pristis
Centaurusque locum tendunt superare priorem;
sentences.l:
After these, with an equal interval, Pristis
and Centaur the place strive to gain, the foremost;
sentences.i: Behind these, level with each other, the Pristis and the Centaur strain to win the lead;
sentences.n: 'aequo discrimine' is an ablative, 'with an equal interval', i.e. neck and neck. 'Pristis… Centaurusque' takes the plural 'tendunt', 'strive', with the infinitive 'superare'. 'locum… priorem' is 'the leading place', the place ahead; 'superare' here means 'to win, to get'.

sentences.t:
et nunc Pristis habet, nunc victam praeterit ingens
Centaurus, nunc una ambae iunctisque feruntur
frontibus, et longa sulcant vada salsa carina.
sentences.l:
and now Pristis has it, now her, beaten, passes the huge
Centaur, now together both, and with joined are borne
brows, and with long they furrow the shallows salt, keel.
sentences.i: now the Pristis has it, now the huge Centaur overtakes her and leaves her beaten, now the two run on together, bows level, ploughing the salt water with their long keels.
sentences.n: 'habet' has 'locum' understood: 'has the lead'. 'victam' agrees with the Pristis, understood as the object: 'passes her, beaten'. The triple 'nunc… nunc… nunc' marks the shifting lead (anaphora). 'una' is the adverb 'together'; 'ambae' is the feminine plural of 'ambo', both ships being thought of as feminine. 'iunctis… frontibus' is an ablative, 'with prows side by side'. 'feruntur' is a passive with middle sense, 'they speed along'. 'vada salsa', 'salt shallows', means simply the sea; 'longa… carina', singular for each ship, is an ablative of means.

sentences.t:
Iamque propinquabant scopulo metamque tenebant,
cum princeps medioque Gyas in gurgite victor
rectorem navis compellat voce Menoeten:
sentences.l:
And now they were nearing the rock and the turning-post were reaching,
when, leading and in the middle of the flood victor, Gyas
the steersman of his ship accosts aloud, Menoetes:
sentences.i: And now they were drawing close to the rock and reaching the turning-post, when Gyas, in the lead and winning at the halfway mark, calls out to Menoetes, the helmsman of his ship:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Iamque… cum' is the 'inverse cum' construction: imperfects set the scene ('propinquabant', 'tenebant', 'they were drawing near, were reaching'), and 'cum' with an indicative brings in the sudden event; 'compellat' is a historic present. 'propinquare' takes a dative, 'scopulo'. 'princeps' and 'victor' are predicative: 'leading, and winning in the middle of the flood', i.e. at the halfway point of the race. 'Menoeten' is a Greek accusative in -en, in apposition to 'rectorem'. 'voce' is an ablative, 'with his voice', i.e. aloud; 'compellat' means 'addresses, calls to'. The speech follows the colon.

sentences.t: “Quo tantum mihi dexter abis?
sentences.l: “Whither so far, I ask you, to the right are you going off?
sentences.i: “Where are you heading, so far over to the right?
sentences.n: The opening mark “ begins Gyas's speech, which ends at 164. 'Quo' is 'whither?'. 'tantum' is an adverb, 'so far'. 'mihi' is an ethic dative, adding the speaker's feeling ('I ask you'). 'dexter' is an adjective where English uses an adverb, 'to the right': Menoetes is giving the rock a wide berth on the seaward side.

sentences.i: Steer over here; keep close in to the shore and let the oar-blades graze the rocks on our left; let the others stand out to sea.”
sentences.n: 'dirige' is an imperative, and 'gressum', 'step', is used for the ship's course (The Latin Library prints 'derige cursum', 'steer your course', with the same sense). 'litus ama', 'love the shore', means 'hug the shore', i.e. keep close in to the rock. 'sine' is the imperative of 'sino', 'allow', with the subjunctive 'stringat' standing without 'ut': 'let the oar-blade graze'. 'palmula', 'little palm', is the blade of an oar. 'laevas… cautes' is 'the rocks on the left': the ships round the turning-post keeping it to the left, as chariots did. The Latin Library has 'laeva', making it 'the left oar-blade'. 'altum', 'the deep', is a neuter adjective used as a noun; 'teneant' is a jussive subjunctive, 'let others keep to the open sea'. Greenough's closing mark ” follows a space, so it opens the next unit.

sentences.t:
”Dixit; sed caeca Menoetes
saxa timens proram pelagi detorquet ad undas.
sentences.l:
He spoke; but the blind, Menoetes,
rocks fearing, the prow towards the open sea's twists away, waves.
sentences.i: So he spoke; but Menoetes, afraid of rocks hidden under the water, wrenches the prow away towards the open waves.
sentences.n: The mark ” at the head of this unit closes Gyas's speech (see the unit before). 'Dixit', 'he spoke', is the usual formula closing a speech. 'caeca… saxa', 'blind rocks', are rocks hidden under the water, unseen; they are the object of the present participle 'timens'. 'pelagi… ad undas' is 'towards the waves of the open sea'; 'detorquet', 'twists away', is a historic present.

sentences.t:
“Quo diversus abis? iterum Pete saxa, Menoete!”
cum clamore Gyas revocabat;
sentences.l:
“Whither, turned away, are you going off? Again make for the rocks, Menoetes!”
with a shout Gyas was calling him back;
sentences.i: “Where are you off to, swinging away like that? Head for the rocks again, Menoetes!” Gyas kept shouting, trying to call him back;
sentences.n: The print has 'Pete' with a capital, a misprint for 'pete' (the word before it, 'iterum', is in lower case); it is the imperative 'pete', 'make for'. A whole speech in one line, opened and closed by the marks. 'diversus', 'turned the other way', is an adjective where English would use an adverb. 'Menoete' is a Greek vocative. 'revocabat' is an imperfect of repeated or attempted action, 'kept calling back, tried to call back'; 'cum clamore' is 'with a shout'. 'Quo… abis?' repeats his first question (162).

sentences.t:
et ecce Cloanthum
respicit instantem tergo, et propiora tenentem.
sentences.l:
and look! Cloanthus
he looks back at, pressing on his back, and the nearer holding.
sentences.i: and then, glancing back, he sees Cloanthus hard on his heels and keeping a line nearer in.
sentences.n: 'ecce', 'look!', marks the sudden sight. 'respicit' is 'looks back at', with 'Cloanthum' its object and the participles 'instantem' and 'tenentem' agreeing with it. 'tergo' is a dative with 'instantem', 'pressing on his back', i.e. close behind. 'propiora', a neuter plural used as a noun, is 'the nearer (waters)', the inside line, nearer the rock.

sentences.t:
Ille inter navemque Gyae scopulosque sonantes
radit iter laevum interior, subitoque priorem
praeterit, et metis tenet aequora tuta relictis.
sentences.l:
He, between both the ship of Gyas and the rocks roaring,
scrapes his path, the left, on the inside, and suddenly the one ahead
passes, and, the turning-posts left behind, holds the waters safe.
sentences.i: Cloanthus shaves through on the left, on the inside, between Gyas's ship and the roaring rocks, suddenly passes the leader, and with the turning-post behind him holds safe water.
sentences.n: 'Ille' is Cloanthus. 'inter navemque… scopulosque' is 'between both the ship and the rocks', with the double '-que… -que' ('both… and', as you have seen before) and 'inter' set before the first. 'Gyae' is the genitive of 'Gyas'. 'radit iter laevum', 'grazes his course on the left', i.e. shaves past the rock; 'interior' is a comparative of position, 'on the inside'. 'priorem' is 'the one ahead', Gyas. 'metis… relictis' is an ablative absolute, 'the turning-post having been left behind'; the plural 'metae' is used of a single post (in the Circus the turning-post was a group of cones). 'aequora tuta' is 'the safe stretch of sea'.

sentences.t:
Tum vero exarsit iuveni dolor ossibus ingens,
nec lacrimis caruere genae, segnemque Menoeten,
oblitus decorisque sui sociumque salutis,
in mare praecipitem puppi deturbat ab alta;
sentences.l:
Then indeed blazed up in the young man a pain in his bones, huge,
nor of tears were empty his cheeks, and slow Menoetes,
forgetful both of his own dignity and of his comrades' safety,
into the sea headlong from the stern knocks down, the high;
sentences.i: Then a huge resentment blazed up in the young man, to the very bone, and his cheeks were wet with tears; forgetting both his own dignity and his crew's safety, he knocks slow Menoetes headlong into the sea from the high stern;
sentences.n: 'exarsit' is the perfect of 'exardesco', 'blazed up'. 'iuveni' is a dative of the person affected, 'in the young man', and 'ossibus' an ablative of place, 'in his bones'; 'dolor' is resentment as well as pain. 'nec lacrimis caruere genae', 'nor did his cheeks lack tears', says by a negative that they were wet (litotes); 'carere' takes an ablative, and 'caruere' is the -ere perfect. 'oblitus', the perfect participle of the deponent 'obliviscor', takes the genitives 'decoris… sui' and 'socium… salutis'; 'socium' is the old genitive plural for 'sociorum'. 'decorisque… sociumque' is the double '-que', 'both… and'. 'segnem… Menoeten' is the object of 'deturbat', 'knocks down', with 'praecipitem' predicative, 'headlong'; 'puppi… ab alta' is 'from the high stern'.

sentences.t:
ipse gubernaclo rector subit, ipse magister,
hortaturque viros, clavumque ad litora torquet.
sentences.l:
himself to the helm as steersman goes up, himself as master,
and urges on the men, and the tiller towards the shore twists.
sentences.i: he takes the helm himself as steersman, himself as master, urges on his men and turns the tiller in towards the shore.
sentences.n: 'ipse… ipse' (anaphora): Gyas takes both posts at once, 'rector', the helmsman, and 'magister', the ship's master; both are predicative nominatives, 'as helmsman, as master'. 'gubernaclo' is a dative with 'subit', 'goes up to the steering-oar'. 'hortatur' is deponent. 'clavum' is the tiller of the steering-oar; 'ad litora', 'towards the shore', i.e. in towards the rock again.

sentences.t:
At gravis, ut fundo vix tandem redditus imo est,
iam senior madidaque fluens in veste Menoetes
summa petit scopuli siccaque in rupe resedit.
sentences.l:
But heavy, when from the bottom scarcely at last given back, the deepest, he was,
now rather old, and in wet streaming in clothing, Menoetes
the top makes for of the rock, and on the dry crag sat down.
sentences.i: But Menoetes, heavy as he was, once he had at last been given back up from the depths, no longer young and streaming in his soaked clothes, makes for the top of the rock and sits down on the dry stone.
sentences.n: 'At' marks the turn to Menoetes, the subject, held back to the end of line 179. 'ut' with the perfect indicative 'redditus est' means 'when, as soon as'; 'fundo… imo' is an ablative of separation, 'from the deepest bottom', and 'redditus' is a perfect participle, 'given back' (to the surface). 'gravis' is 'heavy', with age and wet clothes; 'iam senior', 'already rather old', is a comparative with softened sense. 'madida… in veste' is 'in his wet clothing', with 'fluens', 'streaming, dripping'. 'summa… scopuli' is 'the top of the rock', a neuter plural used as a noun, with a genitive. 'resedit' is a perfect after the present 'petit', 'sat down'.

sentences.t:
Ilium et labentem Teucri et risere natantem,
et salsos rident revomentem pectore fluctus.
sentences.l:
Him both falling the Teucrians and laughed at swimming,
and salt they laugh at him spewing back from his chest waves.
sentences.i: The Trojans laughed at him as he fell and as he swam, and they laugh now as he coughs the salt water back up from his chest.
sentences.n: The print has 'Ilium', a misprint for 'Illum', 'him' (so The Latin Library); 'Ilium', Troy, makes no sense here, and the gloss reads 'Illum'; the line scans only with 'Illum', its -um elided before 'et'. 'Illum' is the object of both 'risere' (the -ere perfect, 'laughed at') and 'rident' ('laugh at'), and the participles 'labentem', 'natantem' and 'revomentem' agree with it: 'falling', 'swimming', 'spewing back'. 'et… et' is 'both… and'. The shift from perfect to present follows Menoetes from his fall to where he sits now on the rock. 'Teucri' are the Trojans. 'salsos… fluctus' frames the line, 'the salt waves', and 'pectore' is an ablative, 'from his chest'.

sentences.t:
Hic laeta extremis spes est accensa duobus,
Sergesto Mnestheique, Gyan superare morantem.
sentences.l:
Here a glad, in the last, hope was kindled, two,
Sergestus and Mnestheus, Gyas to overtake, lagging.
sentences.i: At this a joyful hope was kindled in the last two, Sergestus and Mnestheus, of overtaking Gyas now that he was held back.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Hic' is 'at this point'. 'extremis… duobus' is a dative, 'in the last two', with 'Sergesto Mnestheique' in apposition; 'Mnesthei' is a Greek-style dative of 'Mnestheus', said in the verse as two syllables, Mnes-thei. 'spes est accensa' is a perfect passive, 'hope was kindled', followed by the infinitive 'superare': 'hope of overtaking'. 'Gyan' is a Greek accusative of 'Gyas'; 'morantem', a present participle, is 'lagging, held up'.

sentences.t:
Sergestus capit ante locum scopuloque propinquat,
nec tota tamen ille prior praeeunte carina;
sentences.l:
Sergestus takes the place ahead and to the rock draws near,
nor yet with the whole he in front, going ahead, keel;
sentences.i: Sergestus takes the position in front and closes on the rock, though even so he is not ahead by a whole ship's length;
sentences.n: 'capit ante locum' is 'takes the place in front', the inside position nearer the rock, with 'ante' an adverb. 'propinquat' takes the dative 'scopulo'. 'nec tota… praeeunte carina' is an ablative absolute, 'not with his whole keel going ahead' ('praeeo', 'go in front'; in the verse 'prae' is short before the vowel); 'ille prior' has 'est' understood, 'he (is) in front'. 'tamen' is 'yet, all the same'.

sentences.t: parte prior, partem rostro premit aemula Pristis.
sentences.l: by part ahead; part with her beak presses the rival Pristis.
sentences.i: he leads by part of his length, and on the other part the rival Pristis presses with her beak.
sentences.n: 'parte prior', 'ahead by a part', is an ablative of the measure of difference and takes up the line before. 'partem… premit' means 'presses on the (other) part' of his ship with her beak, i.e. her bow overlaps his stern; 'rostro' is an ablative of means. 'aemula', 'rival, emulous', agrees with 'Pristis', the subject. The Latin Library prints 'partim', 'partly', an adverb, which leaves Sergestus as the understood object of 'premit'; the sense is the same.

sentences.t:
At media socios incedens nave per ipsos
hortatur Mnestheus:
sentences.l:
But in the middle of the ship, striding through his comrades themselves,
urges on Mnestheus:
sentences.i: But Mnestheus strides down the middle of the ship, right among his men, and urges them on:
sentences.n: 'media… nave' is an ablative of place, 'in mid-ship', and 'socios… per ipsos' is 'right through his comrades themselves', with 'per' set between the noun and 'ipsos'; the gangway ran down the middle between the benches. 'incedens' is a present participle, 'stepping, striding'. 'hortatur' is deponent; the speech follows the colon.

sentences.i: “Now, now rise to your oars, Hector's comrades, you whom I chose as my companions in Troy's last hour;
sentences.n: The opening mark “ begins Mnestheus's speech, which ends at 197. 'Nunc, nunc' is emphatic repetition. 'insurgite' is an imperative, 'rise up to', with the dative 'remis': the rower lifts himself off the bench for a full stroke. 'Hectorei socii' is a vocative, 'comrades of Hector', men who fought beside him. 'Troiae… sorte suprema' is an ablative of time, 'in Troy's last lot', its final hour. 'quos… delegi comites' is 'whom I chose as companions', with 'comites' predicative.

sentences.t:
nunc illas promite vires,
nunc animos, quibus in Gaetulis Syrtibus usi,
Ionioque mari Maleaeque sequacibus undis.
sentences.l:
now that bring out strength,
now spirit, which in the Gaetulian Syrtes you used,
and on the Ionian sea and of Malea in the pursuing waves.
sentences.i: now show that strength, now that courage you put to use in the Gaetulian Syrtes, on the Ionian sea, and in the chasing waves off Malea.
sentences.n: 'illas… vires' is 'that strength (of yours)', 'ille' marking what is well known; 'promite' is an imperative, 'bring forth'. 'quibus… usi' has 'estis' understood, 'which you used'; 'utor' is deponent and takes the ablative, so 'quibus' is ablative. The Syrtes are the shoal-ridden gulfs off the North African coast, and 'Gaetulis' (the Gaetuli were a people of North Africa) means simply 'African'. The Ionian sea lies west of Greece ('Ionio' has four syllables, the I a vowel); Malea is the stormy southern cape of the Peloponnese, and 'Maleae' is its genitive. 'sequacibus undis' is 'the pursuing waves', waves that chase a ship. The places stand for the dangers of the long voyage.

sentences.t: Non iam prima peto Mnestheus, neque vincere certo;
sentences.l: Not now the first do I seek, I Mnestheus, nor to win do I strive;
sentences.i: I, Mnestheus, no longer aim at first place, and I am not contending for victory;
sentences.n: 'prima' is a neuter plural used as a noun, 'the first place'. 'Mnestheus' is in apposition to the 'I' of 'peto': the speaker names himself. 'certo' is the first person singular present of 'certo', 'strive', with the infinitive 'vincere'.

sentences.t: quamquam O!—sed superent, quibus hoc, Neptune, dedisti;
sentences.l: although O! — but let them prevail to whom this, Neptune, you have given;
sentences.i: and yet, oh, if only — but let those win to whom you have granted it, Neptune;
sentences.n: 'quamquam O!' breaks off (aposiopesis): 'although, oh (if only)…', and the dash marks the broken sentence; in the verse 'quamquam' elides into 'O'. 'sed superent' takes up again: 'but let them prevail', a jussive subjunctive. 'quibus hoc… dedisti' is 'to whom you have given this', with 'Neptune' a vocative: Mnestheus turns aside to address the sea-god.

sentences.t:
extremos pudeat rediisse; hoc vincite, cives,
et prohibete nefas.
sentences.l:
last let it shame us to have returned; this win, citizens,
and ward off the disgrace.”
sentences.i: to come home last, that would be the shame: win this much, my countrymen, and keep that disgrace from us.”
sentences.n: 'pudeat' is an impersonal jussive subjunctive, 'let it shame (us)', with the infinitive 'rediisse', 'to have come back', as its subject; 'extremos', 'last', agrees with the understood accusative 'nos'. 'hoc vincite' is 'win this', i.e. win at least this much, 'hoc' being explained by what follows. 'cives', 'fellow citizens', is a vocative. 'nefas', 'a wrong, a disgrace', is the object of 'prohibete', 'ward off'. Greenough prints the closing mark ” after the full stop with a space, so the cut leaves it at the head of the next unit, before 'Olli'.

sentences.t:
”Olli certamine summo
procumbunt;
sentences.l:
They with effort the utmost
lean forward;
sentences.i: They throw themselves forward in a supreme effort;
sentences.n: The mark ” at the head of this unit closes Mnestheus's speech (see the unit before). 'Olli' is the old form of 'illi', here nominative plural, 'they'. 'certamine summo' is an ablative of manner, 'with the utmost effort'. 'procumbunt' is 'lean forward', as rowers do at full stretch.

sentences.t:
vastis tremit ictibus aerea puppis,
subtrahiturque solum;
sentences.l:
with the vast trembles strokes the bronze stern,
and is drawn from under them the floor;
sentences.i: the bronze-plated stern shudders at their huge strokes, and the water seems to slide away beneath them;
sentences.n: 'vastis… ictibus' is an ablative of cause, 'with the huge strokes'. 'aerea puppis' is 'the bronze stern', i.e. plated with bronze. 'subtrahitur… solum', 'the ground is drawn from under', means that the surface of the water, the ship's 'floor', seems to slip away beneath her as she shoots forward.

sentences.t:
tum creber anhelitus artus
aridaque ora quatit, sudor fluit undique rivis.
sentences.l:
then thick panting the limbs
and dry mouths shakes, sweat flows everywhere in streams.
sentences.i: then quick, heavy breathing shakes their limbs and parched mouths, and the sweat runs off them everywhere in streams.
sentences.n: 'creber anhelitus', 'thick-coming panting', is the subject of 'quatit'; 'artus… ora' is the object, 'limbs and dry mouths'. 'artus' is the accusative plural of the fourth-declension noun 'artus'. 'rivis' is an ablative of manner, 'in streams'. The last clause has no connective (asyndeton). The race goes on in the next part.
